candidates.teaser: A wave that moved faster than a running horse — and it wasn't water.
candidates.video_title: A City Was Swallowed by Molasses in 1919
candidates.video_description: In January 1919, a massive tank of molasses exploded in Boston, sending a 25-foot wave of syrup through the streets at 35 mph. 21 people died and the city smelled of molasses for decades. This is one of history's strangest industrial disasters.
candidates.script: A 25-foot wall of molasses hit Boston at 35 miles per hour — faster than any human can run. On January 15, 1919, a steel tank holding 2.3 million gallons exploded without warning, burying entire city blocks in sticky, suffocating syrup. 21 people were killed. Horses drowned. Buildings collapsed. And witnesses swore the city smelled like molasses every summer for the next 30 years. So — is this the strangest disaster in history, or does something else beat it?

candidates.topic: Octopus Has Three Hearts and Blue Blood
candidates.teaser: This creature has three hearts — and the moment it swims, two of them stop.
candidates.video_title: Octopuses Have 3 Hearts — 2 Stop When It Swims
candidates.video_description: Octopuses have three hearts and blue, copper-based blood. Two of their hearts stop beating the moment they start swimming, which is why they prefer crawling. Their biology is so alien that scientists studying them sometimes question whether they evolved on Earth at all.
candidates.script: An octopus has three hearts — and the second it starts swimming, two of them shut down. That's why they almost always crawl instead. Their blood isn't red either; it's blue, because it's built from copper instead of iron. They have nine brains — one central and one in each arm, each capable of making decisions independently. Scientists have seriously debated whether octopuses evolved on this planet at all. What do you think — Earth creature, or something else?

candidates.topic: The Dress That Broke the Internet — Color Perception Science
candidates.teaser: Two people can stare at the exact same image — and see completely different colors. Science finally knows why.
candidates.video_title: Why Two People See This Dress in Different Colors
candidates.video_description: In 2015, a single photo of a dress divided the entire internet — some saw blue and black, others saw white and gold. The reason is buried deep in how your brain compensates for lighting, and it reveals that human color perception is far less objective than we ever thought.
candidates.script: Two people can stare at the exact same photo and see completely different colors — and both are right. In 2015, one image of a striped dress split the entire internet. Scientists studied it and discovered your brain automatically subtracts the light it assumes is in the room before deciding on a color. If your brain assumes daylight, you see blue and black. If it assumes artificial light, white and gold. Your eyes don't show you reality. They show you a guess. How terrifying is that?

candidates.topic: The Immortal Cell Line — Henrietta Lacks
candidates.teaser: Cells taken from a woman without her knowledge are still alive today — multiplying in labs across the world.
candidates.video_title: Her Cells Were Taken Without Permission — Still Alive Today
candidates.video_description: In 1951, a woman named Henrietta Lacks had cancer cells removed without her consent. Those cells, called HeLa cells, never died. They have been used in over 110,000 medical studies, helped create the polio vaccine, and have traveled to space — while her family received nothing.
candidates.script: In 1951, doctors took cells from a dying woman without ever asking her. Her name was Henrietta Lacks. Those cells should have died with her — instead, they became the only human cells ever to survive and multiply indefinitely outside a body. HeLa cells have been used in over 110,000 scientific studies. They helped build the polio vaccine. They've been sent to space. Her family found out decades later — and received nothing. Who actually owns your body?

candidates.topic: The Antikythera Mechanism — Ancient Greek Computer
candidates.teaser: A 2,000-year-old device was pulled from a shipwreck — and it could predict the future.
candidates.video_title: A 2,000-Year-Old Computer Was Found in a Shipwreck
candidates.video_description: In 1901, divers discovered a corroded bronze lump near a Greek island. It turned out to be a hand-cranked mechanical computer built around 100 BC, capable of predicting solar eclipses, lunar cycles, and the positions of planets decades in advance. Nothing like it appeared again for 1,400 years.
candidates.script: In 1901, divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze from a 2,000-year-old shipwreck near Greece. It looked like rock. It wasn't. It was a hand-cranked mechanical computer, built around 100 BC, capable of predicting solar eclipses, planetary positions, and lunar cycles decades in advance. Nothing remotely as complex appeared again for 1,400 years. We still don't fully understand how ancient Greeks built it — or why that knowledge completely vanished. What else did they know that we've lost?
